sections.title: Context and Problem Statement
sections.text: To make the CLI tool useful and support shell script linting it is necessary to integrate shellcheck which is quite mature and covers a lot of ground.

sections.title: Decision Drivers
sections.text:
• integration is straightforward
  • embeddable into the application (no dependencies to install for the user)

sections.title: Considered Options
sections.text:
• Link the statically compiled library from shellcheck
  • Use memexec and embed the binary directly

sections.title: Decision Outcome
sections.text: Chosen option: "Use memexec and embed the binary directly," because it does not require to write any haskell or c code.

sections.title: Pros and Cons of the Options
Link the statically compiled library from shellcheck
sections.text:
Shellcheck is written in Haskell and built via cabal-install.

Fortunately the build can produce a static library libshellcheck.a for all supported platforms.

  • Good, because there is no hacky memexec workaround and the memory is shared with the application
  • Good, because no need to parse the output as the data structures can be directly used
  • Bad, because the libraries are not part of an release so they have to be built manually which takes some time and resources
  • Bad, because that makes it harder to embed when done dynamically and when done statically requires a dedicated project to provide them

sections.title: Use memexec and embed the binary directly
sections.text:
On Linux & macOS it is pretty convenient to make a binary from memory executable and treat it like a regular file. For Windows the workaround is to copy it to a temporary folder on usage and deleting it afterward.

Fortunately for Go, there exists a library that does exactly this.

  • Good, because it is super easy to integrate as the binary can be included as is
  • Good, because binaries can be directly copied to the repository, making it easy to build for everyone
  • Good, because there is no need to use the library and interact with Haskell over CGO which allows static compilation
  • Good, because the CLI interface is considerable more stable than the internal library
  • Bad, because version updates need to be done manually by copying files
  • Bad, because the output needs to be parsed again to be usable
  • Bad, because it increases memory usage

sections.title: Context and Problem Statement
sections.text:
Currently, gitlab-ci-verify only supports check written in Golang. This means every check needs to be implemented in Go. This is a high barrier for new contributors and also limits the flexibility of the tool.

Additionally, it makes it basically impossible to add project or organization level checks, as these are highly dynamic and need to be configurable.

sections.title: Decision Drivers
sections.text:
• battle tested solution
  • easy to write and maintain checks
  • support for project and organization level checks

sections.title: Considered Options
sections.text:
• Rego checks, integrated using the Go SDK
  • Interpreted go using yaegi
  • Configuration file using expr

sections.title: Decision Outcome
sections.text: Chosen option: "rego", because it is already well established in the cloud native ecosystem and provides a good balance between flexibility and ease of use.

sections.title: Pros and Cons of the Options
Rego
sections.text:
Rego is a policy language that is part of the Open Policy Agent project. It is designed to be easy to write and maintain policies. It can be integrated into Go applications using the Go SDK.

  • Good, because it is a battle-tested solution
  • Good, because it is easy to write and maintain checks
  • Good, because it supports project and organization level checks through remote bundles
  • Bad, because it requires learning a new language

sections.title: yaegi
sections.text:
yaegi is an embedded Go interpreter. It can be used to execute Go code at runtime. This would allow users to write checks in Go using the same syntax as the rest of the tool.

It is used by traefik to allow users to write plugins in Go.

  • Good, because it allows users to write checks in Go
  • Bad, because it requires learning a new language

sections.title: expr
sections.text:
expr is a library that allows users to evaluate Go-like expressions at runtime. This would allow users to write checks in a configuration file using a simplified Go-like syntax.

  • Good, because it allows users to write checks in a configuration file
  • Bad, because it requires learning a new language
  • Bad, because it is not very flexible and can become messy for a bit more complex checks
